concepts.explanation: Betting that an asset's price will fall: sell borrowed shares now, buy them back cheaper later, keep the difference.
A private investment fund for wealthy clients that uses aggressive strategies, including borrowing and betting against assets.
A bundle of loans repackaged into tranches and sold to investors. Central to the 2008 financial crisis.
Insurance-like contract paying out if a borrower defaults. Lets investors bet on debt failing without owning it.
Home loans given to borrowers with poor credit, at higher interest. Mass defaults on these triggered the 2008 crisis.
Using borrowed money to amplify an investment. Multiplies gains, and losses, relative to the cash actually put in.
A broker's demand for more cash when a leveraged position loses value. Failing to pay forces a sale at a loss.
A central bank creating money to buy bonds, pushing interest rates down and cash into the economy.
A contract whose value depends on another asset, such as a stock, bond or commodity. Options and futures are examples.
How easily assets can be turned into cash. A liquidity crisis means nobody can sell fast enough to pay what they owe.
Government or outside money rescuing a failing company or bank to stop its collapse from spreading.
The first sale of a company's shares to the public on a stock exchange.
A company with no real operations, often used to hold assets, hide ownership or move money.
Buying or selling shares using confidential company information. Illegal in most markets.
A fraud that pays early investors with money from new investors, collapsing when recruitment slows.
Disguising illegally obtained money as legitimate income by passing it through businesses or accounts.
The central bank of the United States. Sets interest rates and controls the money supply.
A prolonged period of falling prices, usually a 20 percent or greater drop, with widespread pessimism.
A prolonged period of rising prices and investor optimism.
Profiting from price differences for the same asset in different markets by buying cheap and selling dear at once.
Investment in young companies in exchange for a share of ownership, betting that a few will grow huge.
Buying control of a company against the wishes of its management, usually by going straight to shareholders.
A company buying its own shares from the market, reducing the count and often lifting the price.
A general rise in prices that reduces what each unit of money can buy.
A significant, widespread decline in economic activity lasting months, typically marked by job losses.
Digital money secured by cryptography and recorded on a shared ledger rather than issued by a central bank.
Money held by a neutral third party until both sides of a deal have met their obligations.
The total value of everything a country produces in a year. The standard measure of an economy's size.
